newsitem.title: USA: New pirates at Disneyland to chase food, not lust.
newsitem.headline: New pirates at Disneyland to chase food, not lust.

text.p: Disneyland, which prides itself on providing wholesome family entertainment, temporarily closed its popular "Pirates of the Caribbean" ride on Monday to purge it of scenes some visitors have complained are sexist.
The makeover, branded by some critics as caving in to political correctness, will take two months.
When the attraction reopens, the automated characters representing buccaneers who raped and pillaged their way across the 18th Century New World will be shown chasing women carrying plates of food.
The scenes that are being removed showed carousing pirates bearing tankards of ale chasing buxom maidens around a tavern.

Susan Roth, spokeswoman for Disneyland, owned by Walt Disney Co, said the 30-year-old attraction had been scheduled for refurbishment. The old animatronics are to be replaced by a computerized movement system, she said.
"Since it was going to be down for a while, we took the opportunity to change a few scenes," Roth said.
Asked how visitors reacted to the scenes of the original attraction, Roth said: "There were a few complaints, and we always listen to our guests."
But Roth denied that Disney's changing the attraction was a politically correct sanitization of the history of lawless pirates.
"They (will) still behave like pirates," she said. Only their lust will be gastronomic rather than sexual.
The ride at Disneyland is scheduled to reopen in March. A similar attraction at Disney World in Florida already features pirates chasing food rather than women.
The Disneyland decision drew ridicule from noted movie critic John Simon, who has railed in the past about the dangers of political correctness.

"It's worse than silly, it's imbecility," he told the Los Angeles Times. "I thought pirates had become so respectable that I would think you'd now have the women running toward them with plates of food."
